title: MB9-21657
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the appellant) is a citizen of Lebanon.
The appellant fears persecution by members of the Hizballah party in Lebanon because he opposed their acquisition of land and property in his region.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the appellant was not credible because of his failure to mention threatening telephone calls, because of an inconsistency in the profile of the agent of persecution, and because of his failure to take any protective measures from the time he received the threats until he left Lebanon. The RPD concluded that an internal flight alternative (IFA) was available to him in Lebanon.

The appellant argues that the RPD erred in basing its conclusion that Hizballah would not pursue him on the fact that they did not target him while he was still in Lebanon and have not attacked his family, who have remained in the village since his departure. He further argues that the RPD erred in concluding that an IFA was available to him in another city in Lebanon.
The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) considers that the determinative issue is whether or not the RPD erred in its analysis of the appellant's credibility.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in determining that the appellant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
My role is to examine all of the evidence and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.1

On June 15, 2020, the appellant received a notice concerning the status of his appeal inviting him to submit to the RAD any documents or observations pertaining to the resumption of deadlines in light of the COVID-19 pandemic. Any such documents or observations were to be provided within 30 days following the date on which he received the notice. As of the date of this decision, the appellant has submitted no observations or new evidence.

The appellant has sworn that the facts on the record are complete, true and correct. His allegations are therefore presumed to be true, unless a valid reason to doubt their truthfulness arises in the course of assessing the evidence on a balance of probabilities.2 For the reasons that follow, the appellant's testimony is not credible. The appellant, XXXX XXXX, failed to mention the telephone death threats from Hizballah

The RPD noted a significant omission in the appellant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), in that he failed to mention the telephone threats he referred to during the hearing. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from this omission.
The appellant acknowledged that he did not mention these threats in his BOC Form, stating that he had not remembered them until the hearing.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. The appellant did not mention the telephone threats in his BOC Form, and this undermines his credibility. In his BOC Form, the appellant devoted 23 lines to describing his life before the events in question, 20 lines to describing the steps he took to come to Canada, and only 12 lines to describing the events surrounding the threats from Hizballah. All of the appellant's allegations concerning these threats are contained in a single paragraph: "In XXXX 2018, when Hezbollah members found out about my involvement against them they threatened me, my family and my children. They told me exactly 'if you oppose our activity again, we will give you a lesson and we are capable to get you even if you were underground'."

The appellant's allegations on the subject of the threats are very brief. It is unlikely that he would forget to mention these threatening calls if he had in fact received them, since he only needed to describe three or four telephone threats and one face-to-face threat. This omission is significant because it concerns the heart of his refugee protection claim, that is, that the threats against him from Hizballah consisted of anonymous telephone calls and one threat made in person by a stranger. The instructions at question 2(a) of the BOC Form are clear: the appellant was to provide all information that is important to establishing his allegations, including the events, dates and places. On a balance of probabilities, the appellant was aware of these instructions, because a lawyer helped him complete the claim form. The appellant failed to mention these important threats in his form; these threats are central to his claim for refugee protection, and this omission undermines his credibility. The conduct of the appellant, XXXX XXXX, is inconsistent with a fear or risk of harm
The RPD was of the opinion that if the appellant's life had been threatened by Hizballah since July 2018, he would have taken other measures to try to protect himself and his family.
The appellant alleged that he had nowhere to go and that Hizballah members did not come to his house because he stayed home at night and went out as little as possible during the day.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. The appellant's credibility is undermined by his behaviour in remaining at home for five months without taking any precautions other than avoiding going out during the day, even though a dangerous organization wanted to kill him. The appellant alleges that Hizballah members wanted to kill him after he and others in his village mobilized against a campaign to acquire land and property in their region. The death threat that prompted him to leave was allegedly made in XXXX 2018, and he left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2019. Thus, he stayed at his home for approximately five months. At the hearing, he explained that he went out during the day only when he needed to, and in his memorandum, he states that he went out as little as possible. On a balance of probabilities, when a person's life is threatened by a group as dangerous as Hizballah, that person will go into hiding to protect their life. At a minimum, if they remain in their own home, they will not go out at all and will pretend they are not there in order to avoid an attack by the agents of persecution. The appellant's decision to remain in his own home, to wait until he had the money he needed to leave, and to even go out on a few occasions is not the behaviour of a person who fears for their life. I draw a negative credibility inference from this behaviour. Hizballah has not shown an interest in attacking the appellant, XXXX XXXX
The RPD concluded that Hizballah was not interested in the appellant because they put no effort into looking for him and have not pressured his family since he left.

The appellant argues that it is not customary for Hizballah members to go after their targets' wives and children and that he would not have left the country if his family had been in danger. He argues that the fact that Hizballah did not attack him between XXXX 2018 and XXXX 2019 does not mean they will not attack him once they realize that the resistance he formed with his neighbours is alive and well and that it is stronger than Hizballah thought it was.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. Hizballah did not attack the appellant while he was at home in Lebanon for five months before his departure. He not only stayed in his own home, but also went out during the day on a few occasions, and nothing happened to him. Therefore, Hizballah had several opportunities over the course of those five months to attack the appellant, and they did not do so. Yet according to the documentary evidence, when Hizballah is looking for someone, even the Lebanese authorities are unable to protect that person.3 If members of Hizballah were trying to find the appellant in order to kill him, they would have found him easily, because they are able to find anyone in Lebanon.4 Moreover, the appellant explained at the hearing that everyone knew where he lived. The fact that Hizballah did not attack him during the five months when he was easily accessible confirms that they have no interest in him and makes it unlikely that they would attack him if he returned to Lebanon. This lack of interest is confirmed by the documentary evidence5 indicating that anyone who is considered to pose an existential or imminent threat to Hizballah's security is subject to close monitoring and neutralization; there is no compromise. If the appellant was a person of interest to Hizballah, they would have attacked him before he left, which they did not do.

The appellant argues that Hizballah does not attack the families of its enemies. The documentary evidence does not support this assertion. The appellant further argues that he would not have left his country if he had believed his family was in danger. However, he states in his appeal memorandum that he [translation] "feared for his life and the lives of his wife and children," as he also wrote in his BOC Form. The appellant is contradicting himself. He is alleging both that Hizballah would not attack his family because that is not their practice and also that he feared for the lives of his family members. This undermines his credibility.

The appellant argues that Hizballah would be motivated to target him if he returned to the country because he was the instigator of the front formed in his village to oppose the sale of land to the organization; he further argues that the fact that Hizballah did not attack him in 2018-2019 does not mean they will not do so if he returns to Lebanon. This is speculation and is not supported by the facts. Hizballah did not attack him and have not attacked his family since he left, nor have they attacked the appellant's neighbours who were also part of the group that opposed the land sales. His wife's family members, who own land and refused to sell to Hizballah, have also not been bothered since his departure. At the hearing, the appellant explained that two of them have left the country, but nothing in the evidence suggests that they left because of any threats made against them. The appellant also stated that three or four other people had stayed, but he did not testify or establish that Hizballah has attacked them either.

Furthermore, the documentary evidence does not support the appellant's hypothesis. Although Hizballah does buy land in that region, according to the documentary evidence,6 they buy land from Christians, not from Sunni Muslims like the appellant and his community. The same evidence indicates that the land is acquired so that it can be sold to Muslims, not so that it can be used for offices and a centre for the party, as the appellant states in his account. In addition, a number of municipalities oppose this type of transaction, although the city hall in the appellant's village chose to do nothing.

The fact that Hizballah has shown no interest in attacking the appellant either directly or indirectly, through his family, and that the documentary evidence does not support the appellant's version of the facts undermines his credibility. The appellant has not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities, that Hizballah has any interest in him and is threatening his life. Final observations regarding credibility

The RPD made no errors. The points noted by the RPD (and the RAD) provide sufficient grounds to conclude that the appellant's credibility has been fatally undermined with respect to the key elements of his refugee protection claim. The appellant is not credible because he failed to mention a key element of his claim in his BOC Form (the telephone threats), because his behaviour was inconsistent with a fear or risk of harm during the five months he remained in his own home with his family, and because he failed to establish that Hizballah has any interest in him.

The appellant has not credibly established that, should he return to Lebanon, he would face a serious possibility of persecution by members of Hizballah, or that he would face a danger of torture, a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment.
In light of this conclusion, it is not necessary for me to respond to the appellant's arguments concerning the RPD's conclusion on the internal flight alternative in Lebanon.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the appellant, XXXX XXXX, is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
